title: Clamp a round-bottom flask on a lab stand
instruction: Clamp the round-bottom flask by its neck in the lab stand's clamp, so that it hangs there clear of the stand's base, without dropping or tipping it, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Setting up glassware on a lab stand (a flask for a reflux, a distillation or a stirred reaction) is routine bench work in chemistry and biology labs and in school science classes, and one of the manual steps that lab automation still leaves to people. This stand carries a spring flask clamp: a spring holds its cork-lined jaws shut, and they open only while the lever on the clamp's arm is held down, so the clamp has to be kept open while the fragile flask is brought in, and the flask must not be let go before the jaws have closed on its neck. One hand can't do both: with one hand on the flask, the jaws stay shut and the neck can't get in.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases, sideways from the midpoint between them, and up from the table top. (1) A lab stand, fixed: a black cast-iron base plate 13 by 33 cm and 1.2 cm thick, its long side running sideways, from 21.5 to 34.5 cm forward and from 5 cm right to 28 cm left of the centre line, and a chromed steel rod 1.2 cm across and 16 cm tall standing on it at 28 cm forward, 25 cm left. (2) A spring flask clamp on the rod: a black boss head (3 cm cube, with its thumbscrew) at 9.5 cm up holds a chromed steel arm (1.2 cm wide, 1 cm tall) that runs from the rod toward the centre line, 9.5 cm up, to the clamp's back, a steel crosspiece 8 cm long (running forward), 1 cm wide and 1.2 cm tall, from 2 to 3 cm left of the centre line. Two jaws run along the crosspiece and close from in front and behind toward the clamp's middle line, 28 cm forward: each is a cork pad 6 mm thick, 4 cm long (from 2.2 cm right to 1.8 cm left of the centre line) and 1.6 cm tall on an 8 mm steel back, 9.5 cm up. A spring (2,000 N/m, up to 15 N per jaw) keeps them shut, 2 mm apart. (3) The clamp's lever: a red steel bar 5.8 cm long, 1 cm wide and 6 mm thick on a bracket above the arm, pivoted 12 cm left of the centre line and 12 cm up and running left toward the rod, with a black rubber pad 2.5 cm square and 6 mm thick on its end. A spring holds it level (about 2 N at the pad, pressed fully). Pressed down 12 degrees (about 1 cm at the pad) it opens the jaws to 5 cm apart; it stops at 15 degrees and springs back up when let go. (4) A 100 mL round-bottom flask of borosilicate glass (90 g): a bulb 6 cm across and a neck 2.5 cm across ending 8.75 cm above the bulb's middle in a lip 3 cm across and 5 mm tall. It stands in a cork ring (8 cm across, with a 4.5 cm hole, 1.5 cm tall) at 28 cm forward and 17 cm right of the centre line, the top of its lip 12.2 cm up. Clamped 4.2 cm above the bulb's middle, the flask's bottom hangs about 1.1 cm above the base plate. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, except that a drop or a tip counts at any time: 0.0 if the flask was ever dropped (falling faster than 1 m/s) or tipped more than 45 degrees from upright. Clamped: the flask upright within 10 degrees and hanging (its bottom at least 5 mm above the base plate), its neck between the jaws and the jaws closed on it (their pads 20 to 30 mm apart, the neck's axis within 7 mm of the jaws' middle line, within their length and at their height within 12 mm). 1.0: clamped, and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre, its TCP, within 5 cm of its start), so both hands have let go; 0.5: clamped, even with a hand still on the flask; 0.25: the neck between the open jaws (pads more than 30 mm apart) at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the flask still. In a real trial all of this is read with a ruler and a side photo (clearance, pad gap, tilt) and from the video (drops, tips, hands).
reset_notes: Press the lever, take the flask out of the jaws and stand it back in its cork ring.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the jaws are two sliders with spring drives (15 N at most); the lever is a sprung hinge, and the task file moves both jaws' targets with its angle instead of a linkage. The stand is one fixed body; its rod is 16 cm, not the usual 50 cm, so it stays below the left arm's path (nothing touches it). The glass does not break (a drop or tip scores 0). Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
